topics.name: U.S. Supreme Court
topics.kicker: Highest federal court · Created by Article III of the Constitution
topics.briefing: The Constitution’s Article III created “one supreme Court” but left Congress to decide almost everything else, including how many justices it would have. Congress started with six in 1789 and has kept the number at nine since 1869. In _Marbury v. Madison_ (1803), Chief Justice John Marshall claimed the Court’s greatest power, judicial review: the right to strike down laws that break the Constitution.
topics.answerHtml: Supreme Court of the United States (accept SCOTUS; prompt on judicial branch or “the court”; do not accept “Chief Justice” or a single justice’s name)
accept: supreme court of the united states
reject: chief justice of the united states
supreme court of the united kingdom

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Senator Oliver Ellsworth wrote most of the Judiciary Act of 1789, which gave this body six members and created lower federal courts beneath it. This body first met in New York City in February 1790, with John Jay as its first chief justice.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this highest court in the United States, created by Article III of the Constitution.

tossups.p: In 1866, Congress passed a law to shrink this body as members left, which meant President Andrew Johnson never got to appoint anyone to it. Three years later, the Judiciary Act of 1869 fixed its size at nine, after earlier laws had set it at six, seven, and even ten members.
tossups.r: Its members are called justices. For 10 points, name this highest federal court in the United States.

tossups.p: In a case about an undelivered commission for a justice of the peace, this body’s chief wrote that “it is emphatically the province and duty of the judicial department to say what the law is.” That 1803 ruling struck down part of the Judiciary Act of 1789.
tossups.r: That case, _Marbury v. Madison_, established this body’s power of judicial review. For 10 points, name this court once led by John Marshall.

tossups.p: The Eleventh Amendment was ratified in 1795 to overturn this body’s decision in _Chisholm v. Georgia_, which had let a citizen of another state sue Georgia in federal court. Later amendments overturned this body’s _Dred Scott_ decision, which had ruled that Black Americans could not be citizens.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this highest court in the United States, which has had nine justices since 1869.

tossups.p: Samuel Chase, who had signed the Declaration of Independence, is the only member of this body ever impeached. The Senate acquitted Chase in 1805, which helped protect federal judges from being removed just for their political views.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this nine-member court, whose justices serve “during good Behaviour,” usually for life.

tossups.p: Architect Cass Gilbert designed this body’s marble home, which opened in 1935 and ended more than a century of meetings inside the U.S. Capitol. William Howard Taft, the only person to serve as both president and chief justice, pushed for that building but died before it was finished.
tossups.r: Its front says “Equal Justice Under Law.” For 10 points, name this highest court in the United States.

tossups.p: Salmon Chase presided over Andrew Johnson’s impeachment trial in 1868, and William Rehnquist did the same at Bill Clinton’s trial in 1999, because the Constitution gives that job to this body’s leader. Rehnquist also added four gold stripes to each robe sleeve after seeing a Gilbert and Sullivan operetta.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this court, whose leader is called the chief justice of the United States.

tossups.p: Justice Owen Roberts’s vote in a 1937 minimum-wage case became known as “the switch in time that saved nine,” because it weakened support for a plan to change this body. Franklin Roosevelt had proposed that plan, which would have added up to six new members, after this body struck down several New Deal laws.
tossups.r: Critics called it a “court-packing” plan. For 10 points, name this nine-member court, the highest in the United States.

tossups.p: Louis Brandeis became this body’s first Jewish member in 1916, and Sonia Sotomayor became its first Latina member in 2009. In 1981, Ronald Reagan appointed its first woman, Sandra Day O’Connor, and in 2022 Ketanji Brown Jackson became its first Black woman.
tossups.r: In 1967, Thurgood Marshall became its first African American justice. For 10 points, name this highest court in the United States.

tossups.p: Under an unwritten “rule of four,” this body agrees to hear a case if four of its members vote to grant a writ of certiorari [“sur-shee-uh-RAIR-ee”]. By law, each of its yearly terms begins on the first Monday in October.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this nine-member court, the final court of appeal in the United States.

tossups.p: Chief Justice Melville Fuller started this body’s tradition of a “conference handshake,” in which each member shakes hands with every other member before they meet to discuss cases. In its oral arguments, each side’s lawyers usually get about 30 minutes.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this highest court in the United States, which meets in Washington, D.C.

tossups.p: The Constitution gives this body original jurisdiction, meaning cases can begin there, in disputes involving ambassadors and those in which a state is a party. In nearly all other cases, it hears appeals from lower courts.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this court, whose nine members are nominated by the president and confirmed by the Senate.

tossups.p: William O. Douglas set a record by serving on this body for more than 36 years after Franklin Roosevelt appointed him in 1939. The Constitution says members of this body hold office “during good Behaviour,” so most serve until they retire or die.
tossups.r: Its leader is the chief justice. For 10 points, name this nine-member court, the highest in the United States.

tossups.p: Writing for this body in _McCulloch v. Maryland_, its leader declared that “the power to tax involves the power to destroy.” That leader, appointed by John Adams in 1801, led this body for more than 34 years, longer than any other chief justice.
tossups.r: That chief justice was John Marshall. For 10 points, name this highest court in the United States.

tossups.p: Under Chief Justice Earl Warren, this body ruled in _Gideon v. Wainwright_ that states must provide lawyers to people charged with serious crimes who cannot afford one. Under Warren, it also ruled in _Miranda v. Arizona_ that police must warn suspects of their rights.
tossups.r: Warren also wrote this court’s 1954 decision in _Brown v. Board of Education_. For 10 points, name this nine-member court.

clues.t: The highest court in the United States and the head of the federal judicial branch
Created by Article III of the Constitution
Nine justices since 1869: one chief justice and eight associate justices
Has the power of judicial review: it can strike down laws that break the Constitution
Justices are nominated by the president, confirmed by the Senate, and serve for life
_Marbury v. Madison_ (1803): Chief Justice John Marshall established judicial review
John Marshall, appointed by John Adams, was chief justice for more than 34 years (1801–1835), the longest ever
The Constitution says justices serve “during good Behaviour,” which in practice means for life
Its building (opened 1935) bears the words “Equal Justice Under Law”
Franklin Roosevelt’s 1937 plan to add up to six justices (called “court-packing”) failed
Thurgood Marshall became the first African American justice in 1967
Earl Warren’s court decided _Brown v. Board of Education_ (1954)
The Judiciary Act of 1789, mostly by Oliver Ellsworth, set six justices; it first met in New York City in 1790 under John Jay
Its size went from 6 to 7 (1807), 9 (1837), and 10 (1863); an 1866 law shrank it, so Andrew Johnson appointed no one
Marshall: “It is emphatically the province and duty of the judicial department to say what the law is”
_Chisholm v. Georgia_ (1793) was overturned by the 11th Amendment (1795); the _Dred Scott_ decision was overturned by later amendments
Samuel Chase, a signer of the Declaration, is the only justice ever impeached; the Senate acquitted him (1805)
Cass Gilbert designed its building; William Howard Taft, the only person to be both president and chief justice, pushed for it
The chief justice presides over a president’s impeachment trial (Salmon Chase in 1868, William Rehnquist in 1999); Rehnquist put gold stripes on his robe
Owen Roberts’s 1937 vote was called “the switch in time that saved nine”
Firsts: Louis Brandeis (Jewish, 1916), Sandra Day O’Connor (woman, 1981), Sonia Sotomayor (Latina, 2009), Ketanji Brown Jackson (Black woman, 2022)
“Rule of four” to grant certiorari; terms begin the first Monday in October; Melville Fuller began the “conference handshake”
Original jurisdiction (cases begin there) over disputes involving ambassadors or states; otherwise it hears appeals
William O. Douglas served a record 36-plus years (1939–1975) after Franklin Roosevelt appointed him
_McCulloch v. Maryland_ (1819): “the power to tax involves the power to destroy”
Warren Court: _Gideon v. Wainwright_ (lawyers for defendants who cannot afford one) and _Miranda v. Arizona_ (police must warn suspects of their rights)

trap.title: The court, not a justice
trap.body: Many clues for this answer name a chief justice (John Marshall, Roger Taney, Earl Warren, William Rehnquist) or one famous justice (Thurgood Marshall, Sandra Day O’Connor). Those people are separate answer lines, and naming one when the question wants the institution loses the tossup. Clues about the Senate (which confirms justices) or Congress (which sets the number of justices) can also tempt you to name the wrong branch.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun: “this man,” “this justice,” or “this chief justice” wants a person; “this court,” “this body,” or “this institution” wants the Supreme Court. Saying only “the court” or “the judicial branch” earns a prompt, so say “Supreme Court.”
trap.line: Real answer line: Supreme Court of the United States (accept SCOTUS or U.S. Supreme Court; prompt on judicial branch; do not accept “Chief Justice”)

topics.name: Tammany Hall
topics.kicker: New York City’s Democratic political machine · Home of Boss Tweed
topics.briefing: Tammany Hall began in 1789 as a social club in New York City and grew into the most famous political machine in American history. Its Democratic bosses won the loyalty of Irish and other immigrants by handing out jobs, food, and favors in exchange for votes. Its most notorious boss, William “Boss” Tweed, stole millions from the city until Thomas Nast’s cartoons and reporting by _The New York Times_ helped bring him down in the 1870s.
topics.answerHtml: Tammany Hall (accept Society of St. Tammany or Columbian Order; prompt on political machine, Democratic Party, or Tweed Ring)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: This organization was founded in 1789 and named for Tamanend [“TAM-uh-nend”], a Lenape chief who, according to tradition, made a treaty of friendship with William Penn. Its leaders took the title of “sachem,” and its meeting place was nicknamed “the Wigwam.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this New York City political machine once led by William “Boss” Tweed.

tossups.p: Aaron Burr used this club to help his party win New York City’s legislative seats in 1800, which delivered the state’s electoral votes to Thomas Jefferson. That success helped Jefferson and Burr tie in the Electoral College.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this New York City organization, later a Democratic machine run by bosses like William Tweed.

tossups.p: In 1835, this group’s regular members turned off the gas lights during a heated meeting, so their opponents lit candles using new friction matches called “loco-focos.” Those opponents, nicknamed the Locofocos, went on to form the Equal Rights Party.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this New York City Democratic organization, later run by Boss Tweed.

tossups.p: A politician from this organization explained the difference between “honest graft” and “dishonest graft,” saying of his own deals, “I seen my opportunities and I took ’em.” Reporter William Riordon wrote down that politician’s talks, which he gave from a shoeshine stand in a courthouse.
tossups.r: That politician was George Washington Plunkitt. For 10 points, name this New York City political machine.

tossups.p: In one cartoon attacking this organization’s leaders, a ring of men each point to the man beside them under the caption “Who stole the people’s money?” The artist of that cartoon also made a snarling tiger famous as this organization’s symbol.
tossups.r: That artist was Thomas Nast of _Harper’s Weekly_. For 10 points, name this political machine led by William “Boss” Tweed.

tossups.p: In 1871, angry insiders leaked secret account books to _The New York Times_, which printed proof that this organization’s leaders had stolen millions of dollars from the city. Reform Democrat Samuel Tilden helped prosecute those leaders, a fight that later helped make Tilden a presidential candidate.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this New York City political machine run by William “Boss” Tweed.

tossups.p: After escaping from custody in 1875, this organization’s most famous boss fled to Cuba and then to Spain, where officials recognized him from a cartoon. He was sent back to New York and died in the Ludlow Street Jail in 1878.
tossups.r: That boss was William Tweed. For 10 points, name this Democratic political machine of New York City.

tossups.p: Construction of a courthouse in Lower Manhattan dragged on for about 20 years while this organization’s leaders padded the bills, paying contractors enormous sums for simple jobs like plastering. The ring behind that scheme included “Slippery Dick” Connolly, Peter “Brains” Sweeny, and Mayor A. Oakey Hall.
tossups.r: That courthouse is named for their leader, Boss Tweed. For 10 points, name this New York political machine.

tossups.p: This organization’s ward bosses won loyal voters by finding jobs for new immigrants, delivering coal in winter, and helping families whose homes had burned. Many of its supporters were Irish immigrants, and starting in the 1870s it was led by Irish Catholic bosses like “Honest John” Kelly.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Democratic political machine of New York City, once run by William “Boss” Tweed.

tossups.p: Richard Croker ran this organization for about 16 years before retiring to Ireland, and Charles F. Murphy led it from 1902 until his death in 1924. Under Murphy, its politicians backed new labor and safety laws after the 1911 Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this New York City political machine that Boss Tweed had run in the 1860s.

tossups.p: This organization helped launch the career of Al Smith, a New York governor who in 1928 became the first Catholic nominated for president by a major party. Another of its politicians, Robert F. Wagner, wrote the 1935 law protecting workers’ right to form unions.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this New York City Democratic machine, whose symbol was a tiger and whose most famous boss was William Tweed.

tossups.p: Mayor Jimmy Walker, a product of this organization, resigned in 1932 during an investigation led by Judge Samuel Seabury. In 1933, voters elected Fiorello La Guardia [“fee-oh-REL-oh luh-GWAR-dee-uh”], a reform mayor who spent years fighting this organization’s power.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this New York City political machine, once led by Boss Tweed.

tossups.p: At the 1884 Democratic convention, Edward Bragg said that supporters loved Grover Cleveland “for the enemies he has made,” meaning this organization’s leaders. As governor of New York, Cleveland had often clashed with this organization and its boss, John Kelly.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this New York City Democratic machine that William Tweed once ran.

tossups.p: In 1894, a state committee led by Clarence Lexow exposed widespread bribery in a city police force tied to this organization. The scandal helped elect a reform mayor, who made Theodore Roosevelt president of the city’s police board.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this political machine, the most powerful force in New York City Democratic politics for decades.

tossups.p: Carmine DeSapio, who led this organization in the 1950s, lost races for district leader in Greenwich Village to reformer Ed Koch in 1963 and 1965. By then, this organization had lost most of the power it held when its bosses ran the city in the 1800s.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this New York City Democratic machine, famous for the corruption of Boss Tweed.

clues.t: New York City’s Democratic Party political machine for well over a century
Run in the 1860s by William “Boss” Tweed and his Tweed Ring
Cartoonist Thomas Nast attacked its leaders in _Harper’s Weekly_
Its symbol was a tiger, made famous by Nast’s cartoons
Founded in 1789 as a patriotic social club and named for a Lenape chief
Won Irish and other immigrant voters by handing out jobs, coal, and favors
Its politician George Washington Plunkitt explained “honest graft”
_The New York Times_ exposed the Tweed Ring (1871); Samuel Tilden helped prosecute it
The Tweed Courthouse took about 20 years to build while the ring padded the bills
Launched Al Smith, the first Catholic major-party presidential nominee (1928)
Reform mayor Fiorello La Guardia (elected 1933) fought its power
Named for Tamanend, a Lenape chief linked to William Penn; its leaders were “sachems” and its hall was “the Wigwam”
Aaron Burr used it to help his party win New York City in 1800
The Locofocos (1835) lit candles with “loco-foco” matches after the gas lights were shut off; they formed the Equal Rights Party
Plunkitt: “I seen my opportunities and I took ’em”; William Riordon recorded his talks at a shoeshine stand
Nast’s cartoon “Who stole the people’s money?” shows the ring, each man pointing at the next
Tweed escaped (1875), was caught in Spain after being recognized from a cartoon, and died in Ludlow Street Jail (1878)
Tweed Ring members: “Slippery Dick” Connolly, Peter “Brains” Sweeny, and Mayor A. Oakey Hall
Later bosses: “Honest John” Kelly (from the 1870s), Richard Croker, and Charles F. Murphy (1902–1924)
After the 1911 Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire, its politicians backed new labor and safety laws
Its politician Robert F. Wagner wrote the 1935 law protecting workers’ right to form unions (the Wagner Act)
Grover Cleveland was loved “for the enemies he has made” (Edward Bragg, 1884), meaning its bosses
The Lexow Committee (1894) exposed police bribery; Theodore Roosevelt then led the city’s police board
Judge Samuel Seabury’s investigation led Mayor Jimmy Walker to resign (1932)
Its 1950s leader Carmine DeSapio lost district leader races to Ed Koch (1963, 1965)

trap.title: Machine or ring?
trap.body: Tammany Hall was the whole Democratic political organization in New York City, and it lasted from 1789 into the 1960s. The Tweed Ring was only the small group of officials around William “Boss” Tweed who robbed the city in the 1860s and early 1870s. Saying “Tweed Ring” on a Tammany question earns a prompt at best, and naming “Boss Tweed” himself is wrong.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun: “this man” or “this boss” wants Tweed; “this organization,” “this society,” or “this machine” wants Tammany Hall. Clues from long before or after Tweed (Aaron Burr, the Locofocos, Al Smith, Jimmy Walker) can only mean Tammany.
trap.line: Real answer line: Tammany Hall (accept Society of St. Tammany or Columbian Order; prompt on political machine or Tweed Ring)

topics.name: William Henry Harrison
topics.kicker: 9th U.S. President · Died one month into his term
topics.briefing: William Henry Harrison became a war hero in 1811 when his army beat warriors of Tecumseh’s confederacy at the Battle of Tippecanoe, and the nickname “Old Tippecanoe” carried him to the White House in 1840 with the slogan “Tippecanoe and Tyler Too.” At 68, he gave the longest inaugural address in U.S. history on a cold, wet day. Exactly one month later, on April 4, 1841, he became the first president to die in office.
topics.answerHtml: William Henry Harrison (prompt on Harrison alone; do not accept “Benjamin Harrison”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: As the Northwest Territory’s first delegate to Congress, this man pushed through a land law in 1800 that let settlers buy smaller plots of public land on credit. He then became the first governor of the Indiana Territory, governing from Vincennes [“vin-SENZ”].
tossups.r: He later won the Battle of Tippecanoe. For 10 points, name this ninth U.S. president, who died after one month in office.

tossups.p: As a young aide to General “Mad Anthony” Wayne, this man fought at the Battle of Fallen Timbers in 1794. The next year, he signed the Treaty of Greenville as a witness, and in that treaty several Native nations gave up most of what is now Ohio.
tossups.r: Decades later, he ran for president with John Tyler. For 10 points, name this Whig who won the election of 1840.

tossups.p: This territorial governor built a brick mansion called Grouseland and, in the 1809 Treaty of Fort Wayne, bought millions of acres from several Native nations. That treaty angered a Shawnee leader who argued that no single tribe could sell land that belonged to all Native peoples.
tossups.r: That leader was Tecumseh. For 10 points, name this governor of the Indiana Territory who later became president.

tossups.p: In November 1811, this man’s camp was attacked before dawn near Prophetstown by warriors following Tenskwatawa [“ten-SKWAH-tuh-wah”], who was called “the Prophet.” This man’s troops held their ground and then burned the town while Tenskwatawa’s brother was away recruiting allies in the South.
tossups.r: That 1811 battle gave this man the nickname “Old Tippecanoe.” For 10 points, name this ninth president.

tossups.p: After Oliver Hazard Perry’s victory on Lake Erie, this general retook Detroit and chased the retreating British into Canada. In October 1813, his army won the Battle of the Thames [“TEMZ”], where the Shawnee leader Tecumseh was killed.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this War of 1812 general who later became the ninth U.S. president.

tossups.p: In 1836, this man was one of several regional candidates the new Whig Party ran against Martin Van Buren, along with Hugh Lawson White and Daniel Webster. He won more electoral votes than any other Whig that year, and four years later the Whigs nominated him alone.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this man who beat Van Buren in 1840 and died a month after taking office.

tossups.p: After a Democratic newspaper sneered that this candidate would be happy in a log cabin with a barrel of hard cider, his supporters made log cabins and cider the symbols of his campaign, though he had been born on a Virginia plantation. They mocked his opponent with the chant “Van, Van, is a used-up man.”
tossups.r: His running mate was John Tyler. For 10 points, name this Whig who won the 1840 presidential election.

tossups.p: Supporters of this candidate rolled huge balls covered with campaign slogans from town to town, which may have helped popularize the phrase “keep the ball rolling.” His campaign was one of the first to win votes with songs, parades, and souvenirs while avoiding clear positions on the issues.
tossups.r: Its most famous slogan was “Tippecanoe and Tyler Too.” For 10 points, name this winner of the 1840 election.

tossups.p: Daniel Webster edited this president’s inaugural address and joked that he had cut out references to Roman officials. Even so, this president, then 68, spoke for nearly two hours outdoors on a cold, wet day without wearing an overcoat or hat.
tossups.r: It was the longest inaugural address in U.S. history. For 10 points, name this ninth president.

tossups.p: This president’s death was long blamed on pneumonia, though some researchers have suggested a different illness, possibly caught from Washington’s polluted water supply, was the real cause. His vice president then insisted on being treated as a full president rather than an acting one.
tossups.r: That vice president was John Tyler. For 10 points, name this first president to die in office, just one month after his inauguration.

tossups.p: This man’s father, Benjamin, signed the Declaration of Independence, and his son John Scott became the only American whose father and son were both presidents. This man was born in 1773 at Berkeley Plantation in Virginia.
tossups.r: His grandson became the 23rd president. For 10 points, name this ninth president, nicknamed “Old Tippecanoe.”

tossups.p: This man briefly studied medicine in Philadelphia under Benjamin Rush before leaving to join the army in 1791. Born before the Declaration of Independence, he was the last U.S. president born as a British subject.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Whig president who served from March 4 to April 4, 1841.

tossups.p: As U.S. minister to Gran Colombia in 1829, this man wrote Simón Bolívar a letter warning him not to become a dictator; John Quincy Adams had given him that post the year before. He had earlier represented Ohio in both houses of Congress.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this man, the ninth U.S. president, whose term lasted only one month.

tossups.p: This man named Daniel Webster his secretary of state and called Congress into a special session that did not meet until after his death. At 68, he was the oldest man to become president until Ronald Reagan in 1981.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Whig president who died in April 1841 and was followed by John Tyler.

tossups.p: Voters angry about the Panic of 1837 helped this candidate win 234 electoral votes to his opponent’s 60. In that election, the Whig Party won the presidency for the first time, and a far larger share of eligible voters turned out than in any earlier presidential race.
tossups.r: He and running mate John Tyler defeated Martin Van Buren. For 10 points, name this winner of the election of 1840.

clues.t: 9th President of the United States (March 4–April 4, 1841), a Whig
Died one month after taking office (April 4, 1841), the first president to die in office
Won the election of 1840 with the slogan “Tippecanoe and Tyler Too”
Nicknamed “Old Tippecanoe” for winning the Battle of Tippecanoe (1811)
Vice President John Tyler took over, the first vice president to become president when a president died

Won the Battle of the Thames (1813) in the War of 1812; Tecumseh was killed there

Aide to “Mad Anthony” Wayne at Fallen Timbers (1794); signed the Treaty of Greenville (1795) as a witness
Treaty of Fort Wayne (1809): bought millions of acres, angering Tecumseh; built the mansion Grouseland
At Tippecanoe, beat warriors following Tenskwatawa (“the Prophet”) and burned Prophetstown

One of several regional Whig candidates in 1836, with Hugh Lawson White and Daniel Webster
Whig chant: “Van, Van, is a used-up man”; giant rolling balls helped popularize “keep the ball rolling”

Born at Berkeley Plantation, Virginia (1773); father Benjamin signed the Declaration; son John Scott was the only American whose father and son were presidents
Studied medicine under Benjamin Rush; the last president born a British subject

Oldest president at his inauguration (68) until Ronald Reagan; named Daniel Webster secretary of state

trap.title: Which Harrison?
trap.body: Two presidents named Harrison show up in quiz bowl. William Henry Harrison was the 9th president, the hero of Tippecanoe who died one month into his term in 1841. His grandson Benjamin Harrison was the 23rd president (1889–1893), who served between Grover Cleveland’s two terms. Saying only “Harrison” earns a prompt, and naming the wrong one loses the tossup.
trap.fix: Tippecanoe, Tecumseh, the War of 1812, log cabins and hard cider, John Tyler, and the record-long inaugural speech all mean William Henry Harrison. The Sherman Antitrust Act, the McKinley Tariff, and the “Billion-Dollar Congress” mean Benjamin. Don’t blurt out “Tecumseh” or “John Tyler” just because a tossup names his enemy or his running mate.
trap.line: Real answer line: William Henry Harrison (prompt on Harrison; do not accept or prompt on “Benjamin Harrison”)

topics.name: Bill Clinton
topics.kicker: 42nd U.S. President · Governor of Arkansas before the White House
topics.briefing: Bill Clinton was born in Hope, Arkansas, shook hands with President John F. Kennedy as a teenager, and became the nation’s youngest governor at 32. In 1992 he defeated President George H. W. Bush and independent Ross Perot to become the 42nd president, the first born after World War II. During his two terms he signed NAFTA and welfare reform, and the federal budget was balanced; the House impeached him in 1998, and the Senate acquitted him in 1999.
topics.answerHtml: Bill Clinton (accept William Jefferson Clinton; prompt on “Clinton” alone; do not accept “Hillary Clinton”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In July 1963, a 16-year-old delegate to the American Legion’s Boys Nation program shook hands with President John F. Kennedy in the White House Rose Garden, a moment captured in a famous photograph. That teenager later said the meeting helped inspire him to enter public service.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this man from Arkansas who became the 42nd U.S. president in 1993.

tossups.p: After graduating from Georgetown University’s School of Foreign Service, this man spent two years at Oxford as a Rhodes Scholar. He earned a law degree from Yale in 1973, then lost his first race, for a seat in Congress, the following year.
tossups.r: At Yale, he had met his future wife, Hillary Rodham. For 10 points, name this Democrat who served as governor of Arkansas before becoming president in 1993.

tossups.p: In 1978, at age 32, this former state attorney general was elected the nation’s youngest governor, but he lost his first reelection bid in 1980 to Republican Frank White. He won the job back two years later and kept it for about ten more years.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Arkansas governor who defeated George H. W. Bush in the 1992 presidential election.

tossups.p: This politician’s long speech nominating Michael Dukakis at the 1988 Democratic convention drew cheers when he finally said “In closing.” He joked about it soon after on _The Tonight Show_, where he played the saxophone, and in 1992 he played the sax again, in sunglasses, on _The Arsenio Hall Show_.
tossups.r: That year, he won the presidency. For 10 points, name this longtime governor of Arkansas, the 42nd president.

tossups.p: After finishing second to Paul Tsongas in the 1992 New Hampshire primary, this candidate called himself “the Comeback Kid.” His campaign film at that year’s Democratic convention was titled _The Man from Hope_, after the small town where he was born.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Arkansas Democrat who won the 1992 presidential election and served two terms.

tossups.p: In 1992, this candidate chose Tennessee senator Al Gore as his running mate and beat both a sitting president and independent Ross Perot, who won about 19 percent of the popular vote. He became the first president born after World War II.
tossups.r: That sitting president was George H. W. Bush. For 10 points, name this 42nd president.

tossups.p: The first major bill this president signed, the Family and Medical Leave Act, let many workers take unpaid time off to care for a new baby or a sick relative. That same year, he created the AmeriCorps national service program and signed the Brady Bill, requiring background checks for many handgun buyers.
tossups.r: His vice president was Al Gore. For 10 points, name this Democratic president who served from 1993 to 2001.

tossups.p: Vice President Al Gore broke a tie in the Senate to pass this president’s 1993 budget plan, which raised taxes on the highest earners. A health care plan drawn up by a task force led by this president’s wife failed to pass Congress and was dropped in 1994.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Democratic president, a former governor of Arkansas and the husband of Hillary Rodham.

tossups.p: In December 1993, this president signed a trade deal with Canada and Mexico that his predecessor had negotiated, despite opposition from many labor unions. During the 1992 campaign, Ross Perot had warned that the deal would cause a “giant sucking sound” of jobs heading south to Mexico.
tossups.r: That free-trade deal was NAFTA. For 10 points, name this 42nd president, a Democrat from Arkansas.

tossups.p: After Republicans won control of both houses of Congress in 1994 with their “Contract with America,” this president clashed with Speaker Newt Gingrich over the budget, leading to two government shutdowns. In his 1996 State of the Union address, he declared that “the era of big government is over.”
tossups.r: That November, he won reelection over Republican Bob Dole. For 10 points, name this Democratic president from Arkansas.

tossups.p: In 1996, this president signed a welfare reform law that replaced Aid to Families with Dependent Children with a new program that set time limits and work requirements. He also used a new “line-item veto” until the Supreme Court struck it down in 1998.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this president, the first Democrat since Franklin Roosevelt to win two full terms.

tossups.p: On the White House lawn in September 1993, this president stood between Israeli prime minister Yitzhak Rabin and PLO leader Yasser Arafat as they shook hands at a signing ceremony for the Oslo Accords. Two years later, his envoy Richard Holbrooke helped negotiate the Dayton Accords, which ended the war in Bosnia.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this former Arkansas governor who served as president from 1993 to 2001.

tossups.p: This president’s special envoy, former senator George Mitchell, chaired the talks that produced Northern Ireland’s 1998 Good Friday Agreement. In 1999, this president backed a NATO bombing campaign against Yugoslavia to stop attacks on ethnic Albanians in Kosovo.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 42nd president, whose vice president was Al Gore.

tossups.p: Chief Justice William Rehnquist presided over this president’s trial in the Senate, the first trial of its kind since Andrew Johnson’s in 1868. In February 1999, the Senate voted to acquit this president.
tossups.r: The House had impeached him in December 1998. For 10 points, name this 42nd president, a Democrat from Arkansas.

tossups.p: This man won a Grammy Award for the audiobook of his 2004 memoir, _My Life_, and later served as the United Nations special envoy to Haiti. With George H. W. Bush, he raised money for victims of the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami.
tossups.r: His presidential library is in Little Rock. For 10 points, name this 42nd president, the husband of Hillary Rodham.

trap.title: Which Clinton?
trap.body: Several famous Clintons show up in quiz bowl. Bill Clinton was the 42nd president; his wife, Hillary Rodham Clinton, was a senator from New York (2001–2009), secretary of state (2009–2013), and the 2016 Democratic nominee for president. Two earlier New York governors share the name too: George Clinton, who also served as vice president, and DeWitt Clinton, who championed the Erie Canal. Saying only “Clinton” earns a prompt.
trap.fix: Arkansas, the saxophone, NAFTA, welfare reform, Al Gore, and the 1998 impeachment mean Bill. Secretary of State and the 2016 election mean Hillary. The Erie Canal means DeWitt, and New York’s first governor is George. When the question says “this president,” answer “Bill Clinton.”
trap.line: Real answer line: Bill Clinton (or William Jefferson Clinton; prompt on Clinton; do not accept “Hillary Clinton”)

topics.name: Amelia Earhart
topics.kicker: Pioneering American aviator · First woman to fly solo across the Atlantic
topics.briefing: Amelia Earhart took her first airplane ride in 1920 and decided right then that she had to fly. In 1932 she became the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic Ocean, landing in a pasture in Northern Ireland. Five years later, while trying to fly around the world with navigator Fred Noonan, she vanished over the Pacific near tiny Howland Island, and what happened to her has never been proven.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: After crossing the Atlantic as a passenger on the plane _Friendship_ in 1928, this woman said she had been “just baggage, like a sack of potatoes,” because Wilmer Stultz did all the flying. She described that trip in her book _20 Hrs. 40 Min._, named for how long the flight took.
tossups.r: Four years later, she made the crossing alone. For 10 points, name this aviator who later vanished over the Pacific Ocean.

tossups.p: This pilot took off from Harbour Grace, Newfoundland, in a red Lockheed Vega and, after fighting ice and mechanical trouble, landed in a pasture in Northern Ireland. When a farmhand asked if she had flown far, she answered, “From America.”
tossups.r: That 1932 flight came exactly five years after Charles Lindbergh’s. For 10 points, name this first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic.

tossups.p: This pilot became the first president of the Ninety-Nines, an organization of women pilots named for its number of charter members. She once took First Lady Eleanor Roosevelt on a night flight from Washington, D.C., to Baltimore while both women wore evening gowns.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this aviator who disappeared with navigator Fred Noonan in 1937.

tossups.p: In May 1935, this pilot made the first solo nonstop flight from Mexico City to Newark, New Jersey. Earlier that year, she had become the first person to fly solo from Hawaii to the U.S. mainland, landing in Oakland, California.
tossups.r: In 1932, she had become the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic. For 10 points, name this aviator nicknamed “Lady Lindy.”

tossups.p: With about 7,000 miles left in a trip around the world, this pilot took off from Lae, New Guinea, in a twin-engine Lockheed Electra on July 2, 1937. She was headed for Howland Island, a tiny speck in the Pacific where a runway had been built for her.
tossups.r: She and her navigator, Fred Noonan, never arrived. For 10 points, name this aviator whose disappearance is still a mystery.

tossups.p: The Coast Guard cutter _Itasca_ waited at a remote island to guide this pilot by radio, and its crew heard her report, “We must be on you but cannot see you,” and that her fuel was running low. A huge search ordered by President Franklin Roosevelt found no trace of her plane.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this aviator who vanished over the Pacific in 1937 with navigator Fred Noonan.

tossups.p: Congress awarded this pilot the Distinguished Flying Cross, making her the first woman to receive it, after a 1932 flight that took about 15 hours. The red Lockheed Vega she flew on that trip is displayed at the Smithsonian’s National Air and Space Museum.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this aviator, the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic Ocean.

tossups.p: Purdue University hired this pilot to advise women students about careers, and a fund set up through the university helped buy the plane she called her “Flying Laboratory.” Her first try at an around-the-world flight ended in March 1937, when that plane crashed while taking off in Hawaii.
tossups.r: On her second try, she vanished near Howland Island with her navigator, Fred Noonan. For 10 points, name this aviator.

tossups.p: This woman was working as a social worker at Denison House, a settlement house in Boston, when she was invited to join a 1928 flight across the Atlantic. The publisher George Putnam helped choose her for that trip, and the two married in 1931.
tossups.r: In 1932, she made the crossing alone. For 10 points, name this aviator who disappeared over the Pacific in 1937.

tossups.p: As a Red Cross nurse’s aide in Toronto during World War I, this woman watched pilots of the Royal Flying Corps train. In 1920, after a short airplane ride with the pilot Frank Hawks in Long Beach, California, she said she knew she “had to fly.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this woman who became the first female pilot to fly solo across the Atlantic.

tossups.p: This pilot took flying lessons from Neta Snook and bought a bright yellow biplane that she nicknamed “The Canary.” In 1922, she flew that plane to 14,000 feet, setting a new altitude record for women.
tossups.r: She later became the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic. For 10 points, name this pilot who disappeared in 1937.

tossups.p: Some researchers believe that this pilot landed on Nikumaroro [“nee-koo-mah-ROH-roh”], then called Gardner Island, and lived there for a time as a castaway, but no one has proven it. Others think her plane ran out of fuel and sank into the ocean.
tossups.r: She vanished in 1937 while flying with navigator Fred Noonan. For 10 points, name this aviator who tried to fly around the world.

tossups.p: This author wrote the memoir _The Fun of It_, and her husband later gathered her notes from a final trip into the book _Last Flight_. She was born in Atchison, Kansas, in 1897.
tossups.r: Reporters nicknamed her “Lady Lindy” after Charles Lindbergh. For 10 points, name this aviator, the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic.

tossups.p: This pilot launched her own line of clothing and a brand of lightweight luggage that carried her name. In August 1932, she became the first woman to fly solo nonstop across the United States, from Los Angeles to Newark, New Jersey.
tossups.r: Months earlier, she had flown solo across the Atlantic. For 10 points, name this aviator who disappeared in 1937.

tossups.p: This pilot finished third in the 1929 Women’s Air Derby, a race from Santa Monica, California, to Cleveland that the humorist Will Rogers nicknamed the “Powder Puff Derby.” Later that year, she helped found an organization of women pilots.
tossups.r: In 1937, she disappeared over the Pacific while trying to fly around the world. For 10 points, name this aviator.

trap.title: Lady Lindy, not Lindy
trap.body: Her nickname “Lady Lindy” and a 1932 Atlantic flight that came exactly five years after Charles Lindbergh’s make the two pilots easy to mix up. Lindbergh made the first solo nonstop flight across the Atlantic in 1927, in the _Spirit of St. Louis_; she was the first woman to fly it solo. Other pioneer women pilots appear too: Harriet Quimby was the first woman to fly across the English Channel (1912), and Bessie Coleman was the first African American woman to earn a pilot’s license.
trap.fix: Listen for “she” and for her last flight: Howland Island, Fred Noonan, the Lockheed Electra, and 1937 all mean her. The _Spirit of St. Louis_ and landing in Paris mean Lindbergh. Say her last name, since “Amelia” alone only earns a prompt.

topics.name: Barack Obama
topics.kicker: 44th U.S. President · First African American president
topics.briefing: Barack Obama was born in Hawaii, spent part of his childhood in Indonesia, and worked as a community organizer in Chicago before becoming a lawyer and politician. A speech at the 2004 Democratic National Convention made him known across the country, and four years later he was elected the 44th president, the first African American to hold the office. He served two terms, from 2009 to 2017, and signed the Affordable Care Act, the health-care law often called “Obamacare.”
topics.answerHtml: Barack Obama (accept Barack Hussein Obama II; prompt on Barack)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: This man became the first Black president of the _Harvard Law Review_ in 1990, and he later taught constitutional law at the University of Chicago. Before law school, he worked as a community organizer on Chicago’s South Side.
tossups.r: In 2008, he was elected president with Joe Biden as his running mate. For 10 points, name this 44th U.S. president.

tossups.p: While running for the U.S. Senate, this politician gave the keynote address at the 2004 Democratic National Convention, saying there is not “a liberal America and a conservative America” but “the United States of America.” He won that Senate race in Illinois against Alan Keyes.
tossups.r: Four years later, he won the presidency. For 10 points, name this first African American president.

tossups.p: This author’s first memoir, _Dreams from My Father_, describes his search for identity as the son of a white mother from Kansas and a Black father from Kenya. Its audiobook won him a Grammy Award, as did the audiobook of his later book _The Audacity of Hope_.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Illinois senator who became the 44th president of the United States.

tossups.p: The first bill this president signed was the Lilly Ledbetter Fair Pay Act, which gave workers more time to sue over unequal pay. Weeks later, he signed the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act, a package of government spending and tax cuts passed during the Great Recession.
tossups.r: He had been elected in 2008 as the first African American president. For 10 points, name this president who took office in January 2009.

tossups.p: In _NFIB v. Sebelius_ [“suh-BEE-lee-us”], Chief Justice John Roberts wrote that a requirement for most Americans to have health insurance, part of a law this president signed, was allowed under Congress’s power to tax. That 2010 law also let young adults stay on a parent’s insurance plan until age 26.
tossups.r: That law was the Affordable Care Act. For 10 points, name this president who signed it.

tossups.p: This president named Sonia Sotomayor, the first Hispanic justice, and Elena Kagan to the Supreme Court. In 2016, he nominated Merrick Garland to fill the seat of Antonin Scalia, but the Senate never held a vote on that nomination.
tossups.r: This president had earlier been a U.S. senator from Illinois. For 10 points, name this president whose vice president was Joe Biden.

tossups.p: In 2016, this president became the first sitting president in 88 years to visit Cuba, after his administration restored diplomatic relations with that country. His administration also negotiated the 2015 Iran nuclear deal, which limited Iran’s nuclear program in exchange for easing economic sanctions.
tossups.r: This Democrat served two terms. For 10 points, name this president from Illinois who held office from 2009 to 2017.

tossups.p: In a 2009 speech at West Point, this president announced that he would send about 30,000 more U.S. troops to Afghanistan. The next year, he announced the end of the U.S. combat mission in Iraq.
tossups.r: In 2011, he ordered the raid in Pakistan in which Navy SEALs killed Osama bin Laden. For 10 points, name this 44th president.

tossups.p: This man spent four years of his childhood in Indonesia before returning to Honolulu, where he lived with his grandparents and graduated from the Punahou [“POO-nuh-hoh”] School. He later transferred from Occidental College to Columbia University.
tossups.r: He was born in Hawaii in 1961. For 10 points, name this 44th president of the United States.

tossups.p: In 2012, this president announced a policy called Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals, or DACA, which let some immigrants who had been brought to the U.S. as children without legal permission apply for protection from deportation and for work permits.
tossups.r: Months later, he defeated Mitt Romney to win a second term. For 10 points, name this 44th president.

tossups.p: Less than a year into his first term, this president was awarded the 2009 Nobel Peace Prize for his efforts to strengthen international diplomacy. In his acceptance speech in Oslo, he discussed when war can be justified, because the United States was fighting two wars at the time.
tossups.r: He was the fourth U.S. president to win that prize. For 10 points, name this 44th president.

tossups.p: In 2010, this president signed the Dodd-Frank Act, which created the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, and in 2015 he signed the Every Student Succeeds Act, which replaced No Child Left Behind. In 2016, he formally entered the United States into the Paris Agreement on climate change.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this president who served two terms with Vice President Joe Biden.

tossups.p: During a long primary race against Hillary Clinton, this candidate gave a speech on race in Philadelphia titled “A More Perfect Union.” His 2008 campaign used the slogan “Yes We Can,” and the artist Shepard Fairey made a red, beige, and blue poster of him labeled “Hope.”
tossups.r: That fall, he defeated John McCain. For 10 points, name this Illinois senator who became the first African American president.

tossups.p: This man met his future wife at the Chicago law firm Sidley Austin, where she was assigned to be his adviser during his summer job there in 1989. Before winning a seat in the U.S. Senate, he served in the Illinois State Senate from 1997 to 2004.
tossups.r: His wife, Michelle, became First Lady when he took office in 2009. For 10 points, name this 44th president.

tossups.p: In 2000, this politician lost a Democratic primary for a U.S. House seat to Representative Bobby Rush. As president, he signed the New START treaty with Russia, which limited the number of long-range nuclear warheads each country could deploy.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this president whose two terms ran from 2009 to 2017.

trap.title: President, law, or running mate?
trap.body: Many of his clues also turn up in tossups that want something else. A question about “this law,” with clues like _NFIB v. Sebelius_, the requirement to have health insurance, or staying on a parent’s plan until 26, wants the Affordable Care Act. Joe Biden was his vice president for both terms and was elected president himself in 2020, so clues about the 2008 and 2012 tickets fit both men.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun: “this law” wants the Affordable Care Act, and “this president” wants Obama. Biden clues: Delaware, a long Senate career, and the 2020 election. Obama clues: Hawaii, Illinois, the _Harvard Law Review_, and the 2004 convention keynote.
trap.line: Real answer line: Barack Obama (accept Barack Hussein Obama II)

topics.name: Battle of Midway
topics.kicker: 1942 U.S. naval victory over Japan · Turning point of the Pacific War
topics.briefing: Six months after Pearl Harbor, American codebreakers figured out that Japan’s next target was Midway, a tiny atoll in the middle of the Pacific Ocean. Admiral Chester Nimitz set a trap, and on June 4, 1942, American dive bombers set three Japanese aircraft carriers on fire within minutes and wrecked a fourth that afternoon. After the battle, the United States went on the attack in the Pacific, which is why Midway is called the war’s turning point there.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Before this battle, codebreakers under Joseph Rochefort confirmed the enemy’s target, called “AF” in coded messages, by having the base there radio a false, uncoded report that its fresh-water plant had broken down. Soon an intercepted Japanese message reported that “AF” was short of water.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this June 1942 naval battle, a turning point of World War II in the Pacific.

tossups.p: Workers at Pearl Harbor repaired the damaged carrier USS _Yorktown_ in about three days so it could fight in this battle, weeks after it was hit at the Battle of the Coral Sea. During this battle, planes from the carrier _Hiryu_ [“HEE-ryoo”] crippled the _Yorktown_, and a Japanese submarine later sank it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1942 battle in which the United States sank four Japanese aircraft carriers.

tossups.p: Ensign George Gay was the only survivor of Torpedo Squadron 8, all 15 of whose planes were shot down attacking enemy carriers in this battle. Soon after torpedo planes like his drew the enemy’s fighters down low, American dive bombers wrecked three carriers in a few minutes.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this battle of June 1942, fought near an atoll northwest of Hawaii.

tossups.p: Lieutenant Commander Wade McClusky followed a lone Japanese destroyer that was racing to rejoin its fleet, and it led his dive bombers to the enemy carriers in this battle. His planes from the USS _Enterprise_ then set the carriers _Akagi_ [“ah-KAH-gee”] and _Kaga_ on fire.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this June 1942 battle that turned the tide of World War II in the Pacific.

tossups.p: At the same time as this battle, Japanese forces bombed Dutch Harbor and seized the islands of Attu and Kiska in Alaska’s Aleutian chain. Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto [“ee-soh-ROH-koo yah-mah-MOH-toh”] planned this battle to lure out and destroy America’s remaining aircraft carriers.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this June 1942 battle, named for an atoll about halfway between North America and Asia.

tossups.p: Henderson Field on Guadalcanal was named for Major Lofton Henderson, a Marine pilot who was killed leading an attack in this battle. Planes flying from the small atoll where this battle took place made several attacks that failed to damage the Japanese carriers.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this June 1942 battle in which the U.S. Navy defeated Japan, six months after Pearl Harbor.

tossups.p: Vice Admiral Chuichi Nagumo [“CHOO-ee-chee nah-GOO-moh”] ordered his reserve planes rearmed with bombs for a second strike on an island in this battle, then changed his orders when a scout plane reported American ships nearby. His carriers’ hangars were crowded with fueled planes and bombs that had not been put away when American dive bombers struck.
tossups.r: Within minutes, three of those carriers were burning. For 10 points, name this June 1942 battle in which Japan lost four aircraft carriers.

tossups.p: All four Japanese carriers sunk in this battle, including the flagship _Akagi_ and the _Soryu_ [“SOH-ryoo”], had also taken part in the attack on Pearl Harbor. Two other carriers from that attack missed this battle because of damage and losses they suffered at the Battle of the Coral Sea.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this June 1942 naval battle, a major American victory in the Pacific.

tossups.p: Admiral William “Bull” Halsey had to miss this battle because of a painful skin illness, so he recommended Raymond Spruance to command the carriers _Enterprise_ and _Hornet_ in his place. Frank Jack Fletcher, aboard the _Yorktown_, was the senior American commander at sea.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this June 1942 battle that Admiral Chester Nimitz’s fleet won near an atoll northwest of Hawaii.

tossups.p: The Hollywood director John Ford filmed the Japanese air attack on an island during this battle, and his short documentary about it won an Academy Award. Movies about this battle came out in 1976, starring Charlton Heston and Henry Fonda, and in 2019.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this June 1942 battle in which American dive bombers sank four Japanese carriers.

tossups.p: Partly to prevent more attacks like the Doolittle Raid on Tokyo, Japan’s leaders approved a plan to capture a small atoll, which led to this battle. On June 3, an American PBY Catalina flying boat spotted part of the approaching Japanese fleet.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this June 1942 battle in which the United States sank four Japanese aircraft carriers.

tossups.p: Japan called its plan for this battle Operation MI, and Admiral Chester Nimitz sent three carriers to wait northeast of the target at a spot nicknamed “Point Luck.” American dive bombers then set three Japanese carriers on fire within minutes.
tossups.r: That attack came on the morning of June 4, 1942. For 10 points, name this battle, often called the turning point of the Pacific War.

tossups.p: The only Japanese carrier to escape the first American strike in this battle, the _Hiryu_, launched two attacks that crippled the USS _Yorktown_. Late that afternoon, American dive bombers found the _Hiryu_ and set it on fire, and it sank the next morning.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this battle in which Japan lost all four carriers of its main strike force, near an atoll northwest of Hawaii.

tossups.p: At the start of this battle, Japanese planes bombed the airfield on Eastern Island and other targets on Sand Island, the two main islands of a small atoll. Japan had planned to invade and occupy that atoll after destroying the American fleet.
tossups.r: Instead, the United States sank four Japanese carriers. For 10 points, name this June 1942 battle.

tossups.p: Raymond Spruance launched his planes early and at long range in this battle, hoping to catch the enemy carriers while their own planes were returning from bombing an island. That night, he turned his ships away to avoid running into stronger Japanese battleships.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this June 1942 battle in which the U.S. Navy sank four Japanese aircraft carriers.

The United States sank four Japanese aircraft carriers and lost the USS _Yorktown_
Called the turning point of World War II in the Pacific
Named for a tiny atoll about halfway between North America and Asia, northwest of Hawaii
U.S. codebreakers confirmed the target “AF” by tricking Japan into reporting that “AF” was short of water
Admiral Chester Nimitz commanded the U.S. Pacific Fleet
Japan’s Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto planned it to lure out and destroy the U.S. carriers

Raymond Spruance (_Enterprise_ and _Hornet_) and Frank Jack Fletcher (_Yorktown_) led the U.S. carriers
Japan lost the _Akagi_, _Kaga_, _Soryu_, and _Hiryu_, all veterans of Pearl Harbor
Came a month after the Battle of the Coral Sea, where the _Yorktown_ was damaged and two other Pearl Harbor carriers were knocked out

Pearl Harbor workers repaired the _Yorktown_ in about three days

Japan also bombed Dutch Harbor and seized Attu and Kiska in Alaska’s Aleutian Islands
Vice Admiral Chuichi Nagumo led Japan’s carriers; switching his planes’ weapons cost him time

John Ford filmed an Oscar-winning documentary there; movies about it came out in 1976 and 2019

The Doolittle Raid on Tokyo (April 1942) pushed Japan’s leaders to approve the attack plan

trap.title: Coral Sea or Pearl Harbor?
trap.body: Three early Pacific War battles share clues: Pearl Harbor (December 7, 1941), the Coral Sea (May 1942), and Midway (June 1942). All four Japanese carriers sunk at Midway had attacked Pearl Harbor, and the _Yorktown_ fought at both the Coral Sea and Midway, so an early buzz on a ship’s name can go wrong. The Coral Sea was the first battle in which aircraft carriers fought each other; Midway was the turning point.
trap.fix: Midway clues: “AF is short of water,” Spruance, McClusky, Torpedo Squadron 8, the Aleutians, and four sunken carriers. Coral Sea clues: Port Moresby and the sinking of the carrier _Lexington_. Pearl Harbor clues: a Sunday-morning surprise attack, the USS _Arizona_, and “a date which will live in infamy.”

topics.name: Battle of New Orleans
topics.kicker: Andrew Jackson’s 1815 victory · Last major battle of the War of 1812
topics.briefing: On January 8, 1815, a British army marched across foggy fields toward a mud wall just downriver from New Orleans. Behind it waited Andrew Jackson with frontier riflemen, free Black militiamen, Choctaw warriors, and the pirate Jean Lafitte’s gunners. The attack failed badly, and the British commander was killed. Strangely, the treaty ending the War of 1812 had been signed two weeks earlier, but the news had not yet crossed the ocean.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: After this battle, Lieutenant Colonel Thomas Mullins was court-martialed because his regiment failed to bring the ladders and other gear that the attackers needed to cross a ditch and climb an earthen wall. That wall ran along the Rodriguez Canal.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this January 1815 battle in which Andrew Jackson defeated the British in Louisiana.

tossups.p: The commander of the attacking army in this battle was a brother-in-law of the Duke of Wellington, and he was killed while leading his troops forward. That commander, Edward Pakenham, had hoped to break through a line of earthworks defended by riflemen from Tennessee and Kentucky.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this American victory that came after the War of 1812’s peace treaty had already been signed.

tossups.p: The American commander in this battle at first called a band of Barataria Bay smugglers “hellish banditti,” but he accepted their help after their leader turned down a British offer and warned the Americans. President James Madison later pardoned those men for their service.
tossups.r: Their leader was the pirate Jean Lafitte [“luh-FEET”]. For 10 points, name this 1815 battle won by Andrew Jackson.

tossups.p: A number-one hit song by Johnny Horton, written by Jimmy Driftwood, retells this battle, beginning “In 1814 we took a little trip.” In its chorus, the enemy soldiers run so fast that the hounds can’t catch them, all the way “down the Mississippi to the Gulf of Mexico.”
tossups.r: Its narrator marches “along with Colonel Jackson.” For 10 points, name this battle that made Andrew Jackson a national hero.

tossups.p: In the weeks before this battle, British boats captured five American gunboats on Lake Borgne, clearing the way for an army to land near a city. The schooner USS _Carolina_ later fired on the British camp from the river until British guns destroyed it.
tossups.r: On January 8, 1815, Andrew Jackson’s army won the main fight. For 10 points, name this battle in Louisiana.

tossups.p: After this battle, the winning general kept a city under martial law and had a federal judge, Dominick Hall, arrested. Hall later fined that general $1,000 for contempt of court, and Congress repaid the fine, with interest, almost thirty years later.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1815 battle won by Andrew Jackson, the last major battle of the War of 1812.

tossups.p: On the night before this battle, Ursuline nuns in a nearby city prayed for its rescue before a statue of Our Lady of Prompt Succor. After the victory, the American commander visited their convent to thank them for their prayers.
tossups.r: That commander was Andrew Jackson. For 10 points, name this January 1815 battle against the British.

tossups.p: On the west bank of the Mississippi, British troops under William Thornton drove back American militia during this battle, but by then the main attack on the east bank had already failed. That main attack crossed open fields at the Chalmette [“SHAL-met”] plantation on a foggy morning.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this January 8, 1815, battle in which Andrew Jackson defeated the British.

tossups.p: The song “The Hunters of Kentucky” celebrated riflemen who fought in this battle, and it later became a campaign song for the general who won it. Free Black militiamen and Choctaw warriors also fought on the winning side.
tossups.r: That general, Andrew Jackson, was elected president in 1828. For 10 points, name this battle of January 1815.

tossups.p: The U.S. Senate approved the treaty ending the war on February 16, 1815, more than a month after this battle. News of that treaty had to cross the Atlantic by ship, so it reached Washington only after word of this battle did.
tossups.r: This battle came about two weeks after diplomats signed the Treaty of Ghent. For 10 points, name this battle that made Andrew Jackson a national hero.

tossups.p: Messengers from the Hartford Convention reached Washington with New England’s demands just as news of this battle and of peace arrived, embarrassing the Federalist Party. In this battle, the defenders fought from behind a mud wall stretching from the Mississippi River to a swamp.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this battle in which Andrew Jackson’s army defeated the British in January 1815.

tossups.p: A tall white obelisk marks the site of this battle, which is part of a national historical park named for a pirate who helped win it. Many of the soldiers on the losing side had earlier fought in the wars against Napoleon.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this January 1815 battle won by Andrew Jackson near a Louisiana city.

tossups.p: For decades, the anniversary of this battle on January 8 was celebrated as a holiday, especially by Democrats. A square in the nearby city’s French Quarter was renamed for this battle’s hero, and a statue of him on a rearing horse stands there.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this battle in which Andrew Jackson defeated the British in Louisiana.

tossups.p: In this battle, the attacking army suffered about 2,000 casualties, while the defenders lost fewer than 100. The attackers had marched straight toward a canal and a mud wall lined with cannons and riflemen.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this lopsided American victory in January 1815, the last major battle of the War of 1812.

tossups.p: Major Gabriel Villeré [“vee-luh-RAY”] escaped from British soldiers who had seized his family’s plantation, and he rushed to warn the American commander that an enemy army was just a few miles away. That evening, December 23, 1814, the Americans launched a surprise attack on the British camp.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this battle whose main fighting came on January 8, 1815, when Andrew Jackson defeated the British.

clues.t: Andrew Jackson defeated the British here on January 8, 1815
The last major battle of the War of 1812
Fought near a Louisiana city on the Mississippi River; it made Jackson a national hero
The pirate Jean Lafitte and his men helped defend the city
Fought about two weeks after the Treaty of Ghent was signed (Christmas Eve 1814), before the news arrived
British commander Edward Pakenham, the Duke of Wellington’s brother-in-law, was killed
Jackson’s men fought from behind a mud wall along the Rodriguez Canal
The main fighting was at the Chalmette plantation; a white obelisk marks the site
Defenders included Kentucky and Tennessee riflemen, free Black militiamen, and Choctaw warriors
Lopsided result: about 2,000 British casualties to fewer than 100 American
Johnny Horton’s 1959 hit song about it begins “In 1814 we took a little trip”
Lt. Col. Thomas Mullins was court-martialed after his regiment failed to bring ladders to cross the ditch
Jackson first called Lafitte’s men “hellish banditti”; President James Madison later pardoned them
Weeks earlier, British boats captured five American gunboats on Lake Borgne (December 1814)
Gabriel Villeré escaped capture and warned Jackson; the Americans made a surprise night attack on December 23, 1814
The schooner USS _Carolina_ fired on the British camp until British guns destroyed it
William Thornton’s British troops won on the west bank of the Mississippi, too late to matter
Jackson kept martial law; Judge Dominick Hall fined him $1,000, and Congress repaid it with interest in 1844
Ursuline nuns prayed before a statue of Our Lady of Prompt Succor; Jackson thanked them afterward
“The Hunters of Kentucky” honored the riflemen and became a Jackson campaign song
Hartford Convention messengers reached Washington just as news of this victory and of peace arrived, embarrassing the Federalists
The Senate approved the Treaty of Ghent on February 16, 1815, weeks after the battle
January 8 was long celebrated as a holiday; the city’s Place d’Armes was renamed Jackson Square

trap.title: Battle, war, or general?
trap.body: Andrew Jackson and Jean Lafitte clues show up in three kinds of tossups: ones that want this battle, ones that want the War of 1812, and ones that want Jackson himself. The same city was captured in 1862, during the Civil War, by David Farragut’s fleet, which is a different event. Jackson’s other famous fight in the War of 1812 was the Battle of Horseshoe Bend (1814) against the Red Stick Creeks.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun: “this battle” wants New Orleans, “this war” wants the War of 1812, and “this general” or “this president” wants Jackson. Farragut or 1862 means the Civil War capture of the city, and Red Sticks mean Horseshoe Bend.
trap.line: Real answer line: Battle of New Orleans

topics.name: Battle of Saratoga
topics.kicker: 1777 American victory in New York · Brought France into the Revolution
topics.briefing: In 1777, British General John Burgoyne marched south from Canada, planning to cut New England off from the other colonies. Near Saratoga, New York, American troops under Horatio Gates, helped by Benedict Arnold and Daniel Morgan’s riflemen, beat him in two battles, and on October 17 Burgoyne surrendered his whole army. The victory convinced France to sign an alliance with the United States, which is why Saratoga is called the turning point of the Revolution.
topics.answerHtml: Battles of Saratoga (accept Battle of Saratoga; prompt on Freeman’s Farm or Bemis Heights)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: A monument at the site of this battle shows only a boot, honoring “the most brilliant soldier of the Continental Army” without naming him, because he later became a traitor. That officer was shot in the leg while leading an attack on a redoubt defended by German troops.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1777 American victory in New York that convinced France to join the Revolution.

tossups.p: After this battle, Congress refused to honor a “convention” that would have sent the defeated army home to Britain, so those prisoners, called the “Convention Army,” were held in Massachusetts and later Virginia. The losing general had insisted on calling his surrender a convention instead of a capitulation.
tossups.r: That general was John Burgoyne. For 10 points, name this 1777 battle, the turning point of the American Revolution.

tossups.p: The Polish engineer Thaddeus Kosciuszko [“kosh-CHOOSH-koh”] chose and fortified the high ground at Bemis Heights for the American army in this battle. Daniel Morgan’s riflemen fought in this battle’s first clash, at John Freeman’s farm, in September.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this pair of 1777 battles in New York that ended with John Burgoyne’s surrender.

tossups.p: This battle wrecked a British plan in which Barry St. Leger [“saint LEJ-er”] would march east through the Mohawk Valley while William Howe was expected to come north up the Hudson River. Instead, Howe sailed off to capture Philadelphia, leaving the main army from Canada on its own.
tossups.r: That army’s general, John Burgoyne, surrendered after this 1777 battle. For 10 points, name this turning point of the Revolution.

tossups.p: Before this battle, John Stark’s militia crushed a German raiding party under Friedrich Baum near Bennington, costing the British army hundreds of men and the horses and food it had hoped to seize. Weeks earlier, that army had easily captured Fort Ticonderoga.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1777 battle in New York where Horatio Gates forced John Burgoyne to surrender.

tossups.p: A tall obelisk honoring this battle has statues of American commanders, including Philip Schuyler [“SKY-ler”] and Daniel Morgan, in three of its four niches, while the fourth niche stands empty. The empty niche stands for an officer who was a hero of this battle but later betrayed his country.
tossups.r: That officer was Benedict Arnold. For 10 points, name this 1777 American victory that brought France into the war.

tossups.p: After this battle, Lord North’s government sent the Carlisle Commission to offer the Americans control of their own affairs inside the British Empire, but Congress would accept nothing less than independence. The defeated British general, who was also a member of Parliament, went back to London to defend his conduct.
tossups.r: News of this victory helped bring France into the war in 1778. For 10 points, name this 1777 American victory in New York.

tossups.p: During the second clash of this battle, the British general Simon Fraser was mortally wounded, reportedly by a rifleman named Timothy Murphy. Fraser had commanded the British advance troops at John Freeman’s farm weeks earlier.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this American victory in New York in October 1777 that ended with John Burgoyne’s surrender.

tossups.p: Baroness Frederika von Riedesel [“REE-duh-zul”], who traveled with her husband’s German troops, described this battle’s aftermath in her journal, including hiding with her children in a cellar during the siege that followed. Her husband commanded soldiers from Brunswick who had been hired by the British.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1777 battle that ended with John Burgoyne’s surrender to Horatio Gates.

tossups.p: Congress removed Philip Schuyler [“SKY-ler”] from command of the army that won this battle after the loss of Fort Ticonderoga. Schuyler’s men had slowed the British advance by cutting down trees and wrecking bridges along the route south from Lake Champlain.
tossups.r: His replacement, Horatio Gates, accepted John Burgoyne’s surrender. For 10 points, name this 1777 battle in New York.

tossups.p: After a bitter quarrel with his commander, one American general rode onto the battlefield without orders during this battle’s second clash, at Bemis Heights, and led a charge until he was shot in the leg.
tossups.r: That general, Benedict Arnold, later tried to hand West Point to the British. For 10 points, name this 1777 battle in which John Burgoyne surrendered.

tossups.p: In this battle’s first clash, on September 19, the British held the field at a farm owned by John Freeman, but they lost about twice as many men as the Americans did. On October 7, the Americans won again at Bemis Heights.
tossups.r: Ten days later, the whole British army surrendered. For 10 points, name this 1777 American victory in New York.

tossups.p: The British general defeated in this battle was nicknamed “Gentleman Johnny,” and years later he wrote a popular comedy called _The Heiress_. His campaign began in Canada and moved south along Lake Champlain toward Albany.
tossups.r: That general, John Burgoyne, surrendered to Horatio Gates. For 10 points, name this 1777 turning point of the American Revolution.

tossups.p: John Trumbull’s painting of the end of this battle hangs in the Rotunda of the U.S. Capitol. It shows a defeated general offering his sword to an American commander, who refused to take it and invited him into his tent instead.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1777 battle in New York, which convinced France to sign an alliance with the United States.

tossups.p: Some officers and members of Congress hoped the winner of this battle would replace George Washington, whose army lost at Brandywine and Germantown that same fall, in a scheme called the Conway Cabal. Unlike Washington, that winner had forced an entire British army to surrender.
tossups.r: That general was Horatio Gates. For 10 points, name this 1777 battle where John Burgoyne surrendered.

Earlier that summer, Burgoyne captured Fort Ticonderoga
The Boot Monument honors Arnold’s wounded leg without naming him

Burgoyne called his surrender a “convention”; Congress refused to honor it and held the “Convention Army” as prisoners
The Polish engineer Thaddeus Kosciuszko fortified Bemis Heights
Barry St. Leger’s march east through the Mohawk Valley turned back at Fort Stanwix
John Stark’s militia beat a German raiding party under Friedrich Baum near Bennington (August 1777)
British general Simon Fraser was mortally wounded, reportedly by the rifleman Timothy Murphy
Philip Schuyler, replaced by Gates, slowed the British by cutting down trees and wrecking bridges
