trap.title: Saratoga or Yorktown?
trap.body: Saratoga (1777) and Yorktown (1781) are the two most famous American victories of the Revolution, and both end with a whole British army surrendering. Saratoga was the turning point that brought France into the war; at Yorktown, French troops and ships helped trap Lord Cornwallis, and that surrender effectively ended the fighting. George Washington was not at Saratoga, so clues about him leading troops in battle point elsewhere.
trap.fix: Saratoga clues: Burgoyne, Horatio Gates, Benedict Arnold’s leg, Freeman’s Farm, Bemis Heights, and the French alliance. Yorktown clues: Cornwallis, Rochambeau, de Grasse, and Washington. Say “Saratoga,” since naming only one of its two fights gets a prompt.

topics.name: Bernie Sanders
topics.kicker: Independent senator from Vermont · Ran for president in 2016 and 2020
topics.dates: Born 1941; elected to the Senate in 2006
topics.briefing: Bernie Sanders grew up in Brooklyn, protested segregation as a college student in Chicago, and moved to Vermont, where he was elected mayor of Burlington in 1981 by just ten votes. He served in the U.S. House from 1991 to 2007, won a Senate seat in 2006, and became the longest-serving independent in the history of Congress. A self-described democratic socialist, he ran for the Democratic presidential nomination in 2016 and 2020.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: This politician was elected mayor of Burlington by just ten votes in 1981, and he later recorded a folk album called _We Shall Overcome_ while serving in that job. He then won Vermont’s only seat in the U.S. House of Representatives in 1990.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this independent senator from Vermont who ran for president in 2016 and 2020.

tossups.p: As a student at the University of Chicago, this future politician joined the Congress of Racial Equality and was arrested in 1963 at a protest against school segregation. That summer, he also attended the March on Washington.
tossups.r: Decades later, he represented Vermont in Congress. For 10 points, name this self-described democratic socialist who ran for president in 2016.

tossups.p: In the 1970s, this politician ran unsuccessfully for governor and for U.S. senator as a candidate of the Liberty Union Party, a small third party in Vermont. In 1991, he helped found the Congressional Progressive Caucus.
tossups.r: He later became the longest-serving independent in the history of Congress. For 10 points, name this senator from Vermont.

tossups.p: In December 2010, this senator spoke on the Senate floor for more than eight hours against a deal to extend tax cuts first passed under George W. Bush, and the speech was later published as a book. He had won his Senate seat in 2006, replacing the retiring Jim Jeffords.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this independent from Vermont who ran for the Democratic presidential nomination in 2016.

tossups.p: As chair of the Senate Veterans’ Affairs Committee, this senator worked with John McCain on a 2014 law that let some veterans see private doctors when Veterans Affairs hospitals had long waits. From 2023 to 2025, he chaired the Senate committee on health, education, labor, and pensions.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Vermont senator who sought the Democratic nomination for president in 2016 and 2020.

tossups.p: In February 2016, this son of a Jewish immigrant from Poland became the first Jewish candidate to win a U.S. presidential primary, beating his main rival in New Hampshire by more than twenty percentage points.
tossups.r: His supporters used the slogan “Feel the Bern.” For 10 points, name this Vermont senator who lost the 2016 Democratic nomination to Hillary Clinton.

tossups.p: The comedian Larry David played this politician on _Saturday Night Live_, and the PBS show _Finding Your Roots_ later revealed that the two men are distant cousins. Both men grew up in Brooklyn, New York.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this independent senator from Vermont who ran for president in 2016 and 2020.

tossups.p: At Joe Biden’s inauguration in 2021, a photo of this senator sitting with his arms and legs crossed in hand-knit mittens, made by a Vermont teacher, became a popular internet meme. He used the image to sell sweatshirts that raised money for charities in his state.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Vermont senator who lost the 2020 Democratic nomination to Biden.

tossups.p: After his first presidential campaign, this politician wrote the book _Our Revolution_, which shares its name with a political group founded by his supporters. His second presidential campaign used the slogan “Not me. Us.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Vermont senator who sought the Democratic nomination in 2016 and 2020.

tossups.p: At the 2016 Democratic National Convention, this candidate asked that Hillary Clinton be nominated by acclamation, ending a primary race in which he had won more than twenty states. He then campaigned for her against Donald Trump.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Vermont senator who also ran for president in 2020.

tossups.p: In 2020, this candidate won the most votes in the New Hampshire primary and won the Nevada caucuses, but he ended his campaign that April as his main rival built a large lead in delegates.
tossups.r: He then endorsed that rival, Joe Biden. For 10 points, name this independent senator from Vermont.

tossups.p: This politician wrote about serving as an independent in Congress in the 1997 book _Outsider in the House_. When he won his first House race in 1990, he became the first independent elected to the House in about forty years.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Vermont politician who later sought the Democratic presidential nomination twice.

tossups.p: As chair of the Senate Budget Committee from 2021 to 2023, this senator helped pass the American Rescue Plan, a COVID-19 relief law, through a process called budget reconciliation. Although he was elected as an independent, he joined the Democrats’ caucus in the Senate.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Vermont senator who ran for president in 2016 and 2020.

tossups.p: This politician grew up in Brooklyn, New York, the son of a paint salesman who had immigrated from Poland, and he studied at Brooklyn College before transferring to the University of Chicago. In the late 1960s, he moved to Vermont.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Vermont senator who called for “Medicare for All” in two runs for president.

tossups.p: During his 2016 campaign, this candidate often said that his average campaign donation was $27, and he relied on small donors instead of a super PAC. He called for overturning the _Citizens United_ decision, which allowed unlimited independent political spending by corporations and labor unions.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Vermont senator who lost the 2016 Democratic nomination to Hillary Clinton.

trap.title: Which progressive senator?
trap.body: Bernie Sanders and Elizabeth Warren were both senators who ran for the 2020 Democratic nomination and both supported “Medicare for All,” so policy clues can fit either one. Sanders is an independent from Vermont; Warren is a Democrat from Massachusetts and a former Harvard law professor who first proposed the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. A different Sanders, Sarah Huckabee Sanders, was White House press secretary under Donald Trump and was elected governor of Arkansas in 2022.
trap.fix: Vermont, Burlington, the Liberty Union Party, or “democratic socialist” means Bernie Sanders. Massachusetts, Harvard Law, or the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau means Warren. Give the last name, because “Bernie” alone only earns a prompt.

topics.name: Bill of Rights
topics.kicker: First ten amendments to the U.S. Constitution · Ratified in 1791
topics.briefing: When the Constitution went to the states in 1787, many Americans worried that it did not protect their basic freedoms, and some states would ratify it only if changes were promised. James Madison answered by writing amendments for the First Congress, and in 1791 ten of them were ratified as the Bill of Rights. They protect freedom of speech, religion, and the press, the right to a fair trial, and much more.
topics.answerHtml: Bill of Rights (accept the first ten amendments to the U.S. Constitution; prompt on amendments; do not accept “English Bill of Rights”)
reject: declaration of the rights of man

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: George Mason’s list of objections to the new Constitution began with the complaint, “There is no Declaration of Rights,” and he refused to sign the document in 1787. Mason’s own Virginia Declaration of Rights, written in 1776, later served as a model for this set of amendments.
tossups.r: James Madison drew on Mason’s work when he drafted them. For 10 points, name these ten amendments to the U.S. Constitution, ratified in 1791.

tossups.p: During a 1789 race for the House of Representatives against James Monroe, one candidate promised Virginia voters that he would support this set of changes, even though he had once doubted that written “parchment barriers” could protect liberty. That candidate won and introduced these amendments in Congress.
tossups.r: That man was James Madison. For 10 points, name these ten amendments to the Constitution, ratified in 1791.

tossups.p: In _Federalist_ No. 84, Alexander Hamilton argued that this addition to the Constitution was unnecessary and might even be dangerous, because forbidding things the government had no power to do might give it an excuse to claim more power. Anti-Federalists such as Patrick Henry insisted that it was needed to protect people from a powerful national government.
tossups.r: James Madison later wrote it to calm those fears. For 10 points, name this group of ten amendments, ratified in 1791.

tossups.p: Congress originally sent twelve amendments to the states in 1789, but only ten were ratified at first. One of the other two, which delays any change in congressional pay until after the next election, finally became the 27th Amendment in 1992.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name the ten amendments that were ratified in 1791 and that protect rights like freedom of speech.

tossups.p: In _Barron v. Baltimore_, John Marshall’s Supreme Court ruled in 1833 that this group of amendments limited only the federal government, not the states. In the twentieth century, the Supreme Court used the Fourteenth Amendment to apply most of its protections to state governments as well, a process called incorporation.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this part of the Constitution made up of the First through Tenth Amendments.

tossups.p: Roger Sherman got these changes added as a separate list at the end of the Constitution, instead of being woven into its text as their main author had planned. That author’s favorite proposal, which would have kept the states from violating freedom of the press, was rejected by the Senate.
tossups.r: That author, James Madison, introduced them in the House in 1789. For 10 points, name these ten amendments, ratified in 1791.

tossups.p: While serving as the U.S. minister to France, Thomas Jefferson wrote to a friend that this kind of protection “is what the people are entitled to against every government on earth.” That friend, who had helped write the Constitution, later drafted these amendments.
tossups.r: That friend was James Madison. For 10 points, name the first set of amendments to the Constitution, ratified in 1791.

tossups.p: One part of this document guarantees a jury trial in lawsuits over more than twenty dollars, and another forbids the government from forcing people to house soldiers in peacetime. Another part says that powers not given to the national government are reserved to the states or to the people.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this collection of amendments that also protects freedom of speech and religion.

tossups.p: Virginia’s approval on December 15, 1791, made these amendments part of the Constitution, and Franklin Roosevelt set aside December 15 to honor them on their 150th anniversary. Massachusetts, Connecticut, and Georgia did not approve them until 1939.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these ten amendments to the U.S. Constitution, written mostly by James Madison.

tossups.p: The words “cruel and unusual punishments” in this document were borrowed from an English law passed in 1689, after the Glorious Revolution placed William and Mary on the throne. The same part of this document also bans excessive bail and fines.
tossups.r: This set of ten amendments was ratified in 1791. For 10 points, name this part of the U.S. Constitution that protects freedom of speech and religion.

tossups.p: North Carolina’s original copy of this document was taken by a Union soldier during the Civil War and recovered by the FBI in 2003. The federal government’s copy is displayed in the National Archives in Washington, D.C., alongside the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution.
tossups.r: James Madison wrote most of this document. For 10 points, name this set of ten amendments ratified in 1791.

tossups.p: One amendment in this group bans double jeopardy, lets people refuse to testify against themselves, and requires “just compensation” when the government takes private property for public use. Another guarantees a speedy and public trial and the right to a lawyer.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this set of ten amendments, including the Fifth and Sixth, which were ratified in 1791.

tossups.p: In the Massachusetts Compromise, that state ratified the Constitution while recommending changes, and several other states followed its example; those suggestions led to this set of amendments. Anti-Federalists had argued that without such protections, the new national government could threaten people’s freedoms.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these ten amendments, which James Madison guided through the First Congress.

tossups.p: One amendment in this group requires that warrants be based on “probable cause” and forbids “unreasonable searches and seizures.” Another begins by saying that a “well regulated Militia” is necessary to the security of a free state.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name the collection of ten amendments that also protects the freedoms of speech, press, and religion.

tossups.p: The House of Representatives approved seventeen amendments in August 1789, but the Senate combined and trimmed them to twelve. The Ninth Amendment, one of the ten that were ratified, says that listing certain rights does not deny others kept by the people.
tossups.r: Those ten were largely written by James Madison. For 10 points, name these amendments ratified in 1791.

clues.t: The ten amendments added to the U.S. Constitution in 1791
Written mainly by James Madison, who introduced them in the First Congress in 1789
Protects freedom of speech, religion, and the press (the First Amendment) and the right to a fair trial
Demanded by the Anti-Federalists, who feared that a strong national government would threaten liberty
George Mason refused to sign the Constitution partly because it lacked a declaration of rights; his Virginia Declaration of Rights (1776) was a model
Congress proposed twelve amendments in 1789; ten were ratified
Ratified on December 15, 1791, when Virginia approved
Alexander Hamilton argued in _Federalist_ No. 84 that it was unnecessary and even dangerous
Includes the right to bear arms (Second), no unreasonable searches (Fourth), and no cruel and unusual punishments (Eighth)
The Tenth Amendment reserves powers not given to the national government to the states or the people
Anti-Federalist Patrick Henry demanded amendments; Madison promised them to beat James Monroe in a 1789 House race
Mason’s list of objections to the Constitution began, “There is no Declaration of Rights”
Madison at first doubted that “parchment barriers” could protect rights
Jefferson, in France, wrote that such protection “is what the people are entitled to against every government on earth”
The proposed amendment on congressional pay was finally ratified in 1992 as the 27th Amendment
_Barron v. Baltimore_ (1833): its protections limited only the federal government, not the states
Incorporation: in the 1900s, the Supreme Court used the Fourteenth Amendment to apply most of its protections to the states
Roger Sherman got the amendments added as a list at the end of the Constitution instead of woven into the text
Madison’s favorite proposal, protecting the press and conscience from the states, was rejected by the Senate
FDR set aside December 15 to honor it on its 150th anniversary (1941); Massachusetts, Connecticut, and Georgia ratified only in 1939

trap.title: Which bill of rights?
trap.body: England’s Bill of Rights of 1689, passed after the Glorious Revolution, shows up in European history tossups, and it gave the American version the phrase “cruel and unusual punishments.” George Mason’s Virginia Declaration of Rights (1776) was a model too. Some tossups ask for one amendment, like the First or the Fifth, instead of the whole set, and others want James Madison himself.
trap.fix: 1689, Parliament, or William and Mary means the English one; Madison, 1791, the Anti-Federalists, or “the first ten amendments” means the American one. Listen for “this amendment” (just one) versus “these amendments” or “this document” (all ten), and “this man” for Madison.
trap.line: Real answer line: Bill of Rights (accept the first ten amendments to the U.S. Constitution; do not accept “English Bill of Rights”)

topics.name: Boston Tea Party
topics.kicker: 1773 Patriot protest against the Tea Act · Led to the Intolerable Acts
topics.briefing: On the cold night of December 16, 1773, dozens of men, many disguised as Mohawk Indians, boarded three ships at Griffin’s Wharf in Boston and smashed open 342 chests of tea. They dumped all of it into the harbor to protest the Tea Act and a tax they had no say in. Parliament struck back by closing Boston’s port, and colonists called those punishments the Intolerable Acts.
topics.answerHtml: Boston Tea Party (accept Destruction of the Tea; prompt on Tea Party; do not accept “Boston Massacre” or “Tea Act”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Shipowner Francis Rotch rode to Milton to ask the royal governor for a pass that would let his ship leave port without unloading its cargo, but the governor refused, and this event began that evening. That governor, Thomas Hutchinson, had two sons among the merchants chosen to sell the cargo.
tossups.r: Men disguised as Mohawk Indians then boarded the tea ships. For 10 points, name this December 1773 protest in which colonists dumped tea into a harbor.

tossups.p: Under customs law, a ship’s cargo had to be unloaded and its taxes paid within twenty days of arrival, or officials could seize it, so Patriots carried out this event the night before that deadline ran out for the ship _Dartmouth_. The _Eleanor_ and the _Beaver_ were also boarded.
tossups.r: Patriots dumped 342 chests of tea from those ships. For 10 points, name this protest at Griffin’s Wharf on December 16, 1773.

tossups.p: Thousands of people crowded into the Old South Meeting House on the day of this event, and Samuel Adams reportedly told them, “This meeting can do nothing more to save the country,” which some took as a signal to act.
tossups.r: Soon after, men dressed as Mohawk Indians headed for the harbor. For 10 points, name this 1773 protest against a British tax on tea.

tossups.p: The day after this event, John Adams wrote in his diary that it was “the most magnificent Movement of all.” He called it “so bold, so daring, so firm” that he considered it “an Epocha in History.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this December 1773 protest in which Patriots threw British tea into Boston Harbor.

tossups.p: Most of the tea destroyed in this event was a black tea called Bohea [“boh-HEE”], grown in China and shipped by the British East India Company. Parliament had passed a 1773 law letting that company sell tea directly to the colonies, hoping to save it from going broke.
tossups.r: That law was the Tea Act. For 10 points, name this protest in which colonists dumped 342 chests of tea into Boston Harbor.

tossups.p: Decades after this event, the shoemaker George Robert Twelves Hewes became well known for telling his memories of taking part in it. At the time it happened, people did not yet call this event by its famous name.
tossups.r: Its participants threw tea from three ships into the harbor. For 10 points, name this December 16, 1773, protest in Massachusetts.

tossups.p: Parliament responded to this event by passing the Boston Port Act, which closed the city’s harbor until the destroyed cargo was paid for, along with the Massachusetts Government Act. General Thomas Gage was sent to govern Massachusetts.
tossups.r: Colonists called those punishments the Intolerable Acts. For 10 points, name this 1773 protest against the Tea Act.

tossups.p: In a later protest inspired by this event, the owner of the ship _Peggy Stewart_ was forced to set fire to his own ship in Annapolis, Maryland, in 1774. In New York and Philadelphia, colonists made tea ships turn back.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this December 1773 protest in which colonists threw tea into a Massachusetts harbor.

tossups.p: The tea dumped in this event would actually have been cheaper than smuggled Dutch tea, but it still carried a tax of three pence per pound left over from the Townshend Acts. Colonists argued that paying it would accept Parliament’s right to tax them without representation.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this protest in which the Sons of Liberty destroyed tea on December 16, 1773.

tossups.p: A fourth tea ship, the _William_, ran aground off Cape Cod and so escaped this event. The three ships that did reach the city, including the _Beaver_, were tied up at Griffin’s Wharf, where the Patriots struck.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1773 protest in which colonists disguised as Mohawk Indians dumped tea into a harbor.

tossups.p: Before this event, the merchants chosen to sell the tea fled to Castle William, a fort in the harbor, to escape angry crowds. Samuel Adams’s Committee of Correspondence helped organize the resistance that led to this event.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this protest in which 342 chests of tea were thrown into the water on December 16, 1773.

tossups.p: Anger over Britain’s punishment of a city for this event led twelve colonies to send delegates to the First Continental Congress in Philadelphia in 1774. Other colonies sent food and supplies to help that city while its port was closed.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this December 1773 protest in which colonists dumped British tea into Boston Harbor.

tossups.p: In October 1774, fifty-one women in Edenton, North Carolina, signed a pledge to stop drinking British tea, in a protest later named after this event. A British cartoon made fun of those women.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1773 protest in which the Sons of Liberty dumped tea into Boston Harbor.

tossups.p: Right after this event, Paul Revere rode from his city to New York and Philadelphia to spread the news. Revere is thought to have taken part himself, and many of the participants smeared soot or coal dust on their faces as a disguise.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this December 1773 protest in which Patriots dressed as Mohawks dumped British tea.

tossups.p: Benjamin Franklin, who was living in London, thought the city responsible for this event should repay the East India Company for the property destroyed. When news of this event reached London in January 1774, Lord North’s government decided to punish the city.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this protest in which colonists dumped 342 chests of tea into Boston Harbor on December 16, 1773.

trap.title: Event, law, or punishment?
trap.body: Three answers travel together: the Tea Act (May 1773), the law that let the East India Company sell tea directly to the colonies; the Boston Tea Party (December 1773), the protest; and the Coercive or Intolerable Acts (1774), Parliament’s punishment. Clues like Lord North, the East India Company, and the Boston Port Act can show up in all three kinds of tossups. The Boston Massacre (1770), from the same city, is a fourth trap.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun: “this law” or “these acts” wants the Tea Act or the Intolerable Acts, and “this event” or “this protest” wants the Boston Tea Party. Mohawk disguises, Griffin’s Wharf, and the _Dartmouth_ mean the Tea Party; King Street and Crispus Attucks mean the Massacre.
trap.line: Real answer line: Boston Tea Party (do not accept “Boston Massacre”)
